title: Delay of inclusionary zoning rejected on tie
subtitle: Committee heard market analysis, affordable housing programs and Housing Accelerator Fund commitments; refusal goes to Council on December 16.
overview: The committee considered a staff recommendation to delay Kitchener's inclusionary zoning policy in protected major transit station areas from January 2025 to January 2026. Inclusionary zoning requires some new units in developments to be affordable. Staff relied on a consultant's updated market analysis showing weak condominium sales, high construction and borrowing costs, and a development industry asking for a delay.

The motion to adopt the Official Plan and Zoning By-law amendments was lost on a tie {{vote:m1}}. As a result, the amendments are treated as refused. A refusal motion will go to the December 16, 2024 Council meeting for ratification, so the final outcome is not yet settled.

For residents, the tie means the delay was not recommended by the committee, though Council has the final say. Staff said the policy would be expected to produce only a small number of affordable units a year at first. Fifteen delegates were registered for a separate item, and several speakers at this item urged the committee to keep the original 2025 start date.

decisions.detail: A motion to adopt the Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment moving the start of inclusionary zoning to January 1, 2026 was lost on a tie {{vote:m1}}, so the amendments are effectively refused and a refusal motion goes to Council on December 16, 2024.

debate: Supporters of the delay, including the consultant and some councillors, said development economics are strained by high construction and borrowing costs and weak sales. They argued that even a small affordable-unit requirement could stop projects from being financed and built.

Delegates opposed to the delay said Council set the policy unanimously in March 2024 and that housing need and homelessness have grown since. They said the market analysis drew mainly on the development industry and that falling interest rates and easing construction costs weaken the case for waiting.

Some councillors argued the city has limited jurisdiction over affordable housing and has already offered many measures, including fee exemptions, reduced parking requirements and land donations. Others replied that municipalities are the only level of government that can adopt inclusionary zoning and that it is one of few tools available.

Staff said the Housing Accelerator Fund commitment of 21 inclusionary zoning units could be reassigned to another initiative, with a request made to the federal housing agency and approval expected but not confirmed. Staff also said the policy would still apply to projects that get building permits in 2026 or later.
Several councillors said the decision was difficult, with concern about both the urgency of housing need and the risk of stalling new housing starts in a weak market.
